description: We are not neccesarily looking for specific skills but we would really appreciate people who know how to code or good at statistics. We are a versatile team founded by 3 people: Deniz Elguş, Kağan Karakaya and Deniz Akçura. We are a versatile team and 2 people here has a past of coding. Turkish is our native language but we can also speak English fluently.
summary: Project Barışçıl is a first-person 3D game in which the player designs a complete crewed space mission and then flies it. At a launch base on Earth the player walks between seven stations: they stack a rocket from parts using engines NASA actually flew (F-1, J-2, RS-25, RL10 and more), or design their own engine; choose avionics; train a landing autopilot with a real reinforcement-learning loop by writing its rewards and penalties; pick and train astronauts; and load the base modules to carry. Every choice costs budget and obeys real physics: stage delta-v comes from the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, and custom engines are computed from isentropic nozzle flow. A flight-controller GO/NO-GO poll checks the design before launch. The mission then plays out: countdown, staging, the transfer to the Moon or Mars, a landing flown by the AI the player trained, and first-person construction of the surface base, ending in a scored mission report. A guided tour explains every step in about three minutes. The game shows why mission design is a chain of trade-offs between mass, power, cost and risk, and makes those trade-offs playable.
details:
**What it does.** The player runs a mission from an Earth launch base to a base on the Moon (Shackleton crater rim) or Mars (Jezero crater), inside a fixed budget.

- **Vehicle Assembly Building:** stack capsule, tanks, engines, decouplers, cargo bay, landing legs and heat shield. The game computes mass, thrust-to-weight and delta-v per stage, handles parallel staging with solid boosters, and assigns each stage's delta-v to the mission phases (ascent, transfer, orbit insertion, landing).

- **Engine Test Center:** design a liquid engine by choosing propellant, power cycle, chamber pressure and expansion ratio. Thrust coefficient and specific impulse come from isentropic nozzle relations; development costs R&D budget and hot-fire tests raise reliability.

- **Avionics Lab:** flight computer, sensors, communications and redundancy. The computer sets how finely the landing AI can represent the world; the sensors set how noisy its readings are.

- **AI Training Lab:** a tabular Q-learning landing autopilot. The player sets the reward for a soft landing and the penalties for crashing, fuel use and time, buys training episodes, watches attempts and can reward or punish them by hand. A policy map shows the braking strategy the agent learned.

- **Astronaut Training Center:** choose crew, create astronauts by distributing skill points, and send them through training programs. Piloting skill decides whether the commander can save a landing when the AI fails.

- **Payload Processing:** choose base modules (habitat, power, life support, comms, ISRU and more), limited by cargo slots, mass and budget.

- **Mission Control:** a GO/NO-GO poll of twelve flight-control consoles, then launch, transfer, AI-flown landing, first-person base building and a scored mission report.

**Why it matters.** It turns the trade-offs of mission design (mass against delta-v, capability against cost, autonomy against signal delay) into decisions the player feels, and it shows reinforcement learning as something a player shapes through rewards rather than a black box.

**Tools.** Unity 6 (Universal Render Pipeline), C#. All 3D models, textures, sounds and music are generated procedurally by the game's own code at runtime; there are no downloaded art or audio assets. Interface in Turkish and English.

**What we considered.** Physical plausibility over spectacle; a visual style based on white, black, orange and blue; a guided tour and a one-click recommended setup at every station so a first-time player can finish a mission in a few minutes.

**Honest limits.** Engine and mission figures are rounded values from public NASA sources and are approximate. The ascent is not a trajectory simulation: feasibility is decided by the delta-v budget. The landing is one-dimensional (altitude and vertical speed).
